notes: With-skill: 100% ± 0% pass vs baseline 81% ± 20%, delta +0.19. The skill also ran ~9s FASTER (50.7s vs 59.5s) at +3.5k tokens (~12%): it makes the model more directed (less flailing) while producing richer output.

Eval-1 (razor-anchoring) is NON-DISCRIMINATING: both arms scored 5/5 because the prompt itself said 'grounded in THIS actual component', so the baseline anchored too. The skill's auto-anchoring behavior never got a fair test. Iteration-2 fix: add an eval where the user does NOT explicitly demand anchoring (e.g. 'I'm working on this file, give me prompts to improve it') to see if the skill grounds in real context on its own.

All three eval prompts literally say 'Socratic prompt(s)', so baselines are strong (the model already knows the technique). The skill's repeatable wins are DISCIPLINE, not teaching: (a) naming real established frameworks (AIDA/PAS/Diataxis/WCAG SC numbers) vs. asking the model to derive criteria; (b) always emitting the reusable skeleton; (c) staying concise/paste-ready instead of building heavy multi-stage mega-prompts.

Variance is entirely in the baseline, driven by eval-2 (0.6): the baseline drifted into a 5-stage imperative prompt, named no framework, and left no literal placeholder. With-skill held 100% with zero variance across all three.

Weakly-discriminating assertion: 'output is prompts, not the task itself' passed in all 6 runs — keep it as a guardrail but it doesn't separate the configs. The differentiating assertions were 'names a real framework', 'ends with a reusable skeleton', and 'leaves a bracketed placeholder'.
